audited.problem: The description sends the dumbbells 'toward your hips,' but every sourced version of this row pulls them up toward the lower ribs/chest with the elbows driving back, not down toward the hips. On a chest-supported incline row there is no hip to pull toward — the torso is pinned flat to the bench the whole rep.

proposed.cue: Chest on the incline, row the dumbbells up toward your ribs.
proposed.description: Lie chest-down on an incline bench with a dumbbell in each hand hanging down. Row them up toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back, squeezing your shoulder blades, then lower slowly. The supported position isolates the mid-back cleanly.

audited.problem: The description has you stand upright facing the cable the whole rep. Every sourced version of a cable pullover hinges forward at the hips about 30-45 degrees with the arms reaching overhead in line with the cable — that forward hinge is what gives the exercise its long lat stretch and is the one thing that tells it apart from a straight-arm pulldown (which is done standing tall). As written, this card describes the same body position as straight-arm-cable-pulldown, just with the arms starting slightly bent instead of straight.

proposed.cue: Hinge forward at the hips, then sweep the bar down to your thighs with straight-ish arms.
proposed.description: Hinge forward at the hips about 30 to 45 degrees with soft knees and a braced core, then reach the bar straight overhead in line with the cable. Keeping your arms nearly straight, sweep it down in an arc to your thighs using your lats, then return under control to the stretch. The forward hinge is what gives this move its long stretch — stand upright and you are just doing a straight-arm pulldown.

audited.problem: The description has the lifter's chest against a pad, with the pad credited for keeping the lower back safe. The plain seated row machine (distinct from this same batch's chest-supported-row-machine) has a foot platform, not a chest pad — feet planted, knees soft, torso held upright by the lifter's own core and lower back, not by a pad. As written, this card describes the exact feature that is supposed to separate it from chest-supported-row-machine, so the two converge on the same setup.

proposed.cue: Feet braced on the platform, pull the handles to your torso without rocking.
proposed.description: Sit at the row machine with your feet planted on the footplate, knees slightly bent, and grip the handles with your torso upright and arms extended. Pull them toward your torso by driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return slowly over 2-3 seconds. There is no chest pad on this machine — your own core and lower back hold the torso still, which is what tells it apart from the chest-supported row.

audited.problem: The cue and description raise the dumbbells to the front first, then sweep out to the sides, then overhead. Both sourced guides run the opposite order: lateral (side) raise first, then bring the dumbbells in to the front, then press overhead, then reverse. Swapping the first two phases changes which head of the deltoid takes the first, heaviest part of the lift -- the whole point of a '6-way' raise is hitting all three heads in a fixed, trained sequence.

proposed.cue: Raise out to the sides, sweep to the front, then press overhead -- and reverse.
proposed.description: Raise the dumbbells out to the sides to shoulder height, sweep them in to the front at the same height, then press overhead, and reverse the path back down -- that's one rep. It hits the side, front, and rear shoulders in a single flowing set. Use very light weights.

audited.note: 'L-raise' names at least three different movements online and sources disagree with each other, not just with the card. Virtuagym's 'Dumbbells L-raise (alternating)' is a plain lateral raise with no rotation at all. The rotator-cuff sources describe a static L position -- upper arm held at shoulder height, elbow bent 90 degrees, the whole time -- where only the forearm rotates from pointing down to pointing up; the arm never travels from the side up to shoulder height as part of the rep. The shipped card describes a third thing: raise the straight arm from the side up to shoulder height, then bend the elbow and rotate the forearm up. That compound two-phase version is not clearly attested by any single source found, so this is not a confident fix -- writing a 'proposed' correction would mean picking one of two unrelated real exercises to replace it with, and either guess could be wrong. Flagging rather than fixing.

audited.problem: The cue and description both say to keep the arms straight throughout the T-fly ('lean back with straight arms...keeping them straight, pull your hands out'). Both sourced guides specifically call for a slight bend in the elbows, and warn that locking the arms straight is a form error -- the opposite error they warn against is bending the elbows too much, which turns the fly into a row. The shipped TRX Y-raise card (same batch) correctly keeps straight arms, because that is a genuinely different movement; the T-fly is not.

proposed.cue: Lean back and pull your arms out to the sides in a T, elbows softly bent.
proposed.description: Hold the TRX handles and lean back with arms extended, a slight bend in the elbows. Keeping that same soft bend, pull your hands out to the sides into a T, squeezing your shoulder blades, then return slowly. A bodyweight reverse fly for the rear shoulders -- adjust the lean for difficulty.

audited.problem: Shipped as a bodyweight move -- equipment is ['bench'] only (no dumbbell/barbell), and its own alias is 'Bodyweight Skull Crusher' -- but the cue and description say 'holding a weight over your chest' and 'lower the weight toward your forehead,' which describes the WEIGHTED skull crusher (the separate dumbbell-skull-crusher card just below it in EXERCISES order). Every sourced bodyweight skull crusher instead has the lifter grip a waist-high bar or bench edge, walk the feet back into a straight plank, and lower the forehead toward the hands using only bodyweight -- the same shape as this batch's own bodyweight-triceps-extension card.

proposed.cue: Grip a waist-high bar or bench, walk your feet back into a plank, and lower your head toward your hands.
proposed.description: Grip a stable waist-height bar or bench edge with an overhand grip and walk your feet back until your body forms a straight plank. Keeping your upper arms still, bend your elbows to lower your forehead toward your hands, then press back up to straighten your arms. No weight is used -- your own bodyweight supplies the resistance.

audited.note: Every sourced guide treats 'belt squat' and 'pendulum squat' as two distinct machines, not two names for one thing. A belt squat loads the hips through a belt with hands free and no shoulder contact; a pendulum squat has the lifter push shoulders into pads and guide the load through an arc, same shoulder-loading family as this library's own hack-squat-machine. The shipped card is named 'Pendulum Belt Squat' (aliased 'Belt Squat') but its cue and description describe only the hip-belt version -- hands-free, no shoulder pads, no arc motion named anywhere. One source does show a niche 'belt-and-pendulum squat attachment' that mounts to a rig and genuinely combines both, but that is an uncommon accessory, not what most gyms mean by either name alone. Not a confident fix: it could mean renaming to plain 'Belt Squat' to match the existing text, or rewriting the text to describe the shoulder-pad pendulum arc instead, or being the rare hybrid attachment as named -- three different real answers, and nothing in the shipped card signals which was intended. Flagging rather than guessing.

audited.problem: The card describes only a hip hinge down and a vague 'curl back up,' with no knee movement named anywhere. Both sourced guides (Muscle & Strength's step list and the exercise's originating peer-reviewed paper, McCall et al., JSCR 2009) agree the razor curl starts in a deep crouch with hips AND knees both bent, then extends hip and knee together to reach a straight, parallel-to-floor line, and returns by flexing hip and knee together using the hamstrings. The simultaneous knee action is the 'curl' the name refers to, and the shipped text omits it, describing something closer to a hip-hinge-only reverse hyper instead.

proposed.cue: Crouch with hips and knees bent, ankles anchored, then push your body straight out using your hips and hamstrings.
proposed.description: Kneel with your ankles anchored and sit back onto your heels so your hips and knees are both deeply bent. Extend your hips and knees together to push your body out into a straight line, then pull yourself back to the start by bending your hips and knees together, using your hamstrings. Starting from this bent crouch makes it a touch more doable than a full Nordic curl, which starts upright.

audited.note: Every dumbbell-leg-curl guide found (thefitnessphantom, dmoose, gymgeek, and others checked) describes the dumbbell-between-the-feet version as PRONE only -- lie face down on a bench, knees at the edge, curl the dumbbell up toward the glutes. None describes a seated version done the way this card does: sit on the edge of a bench, legs extended, dumbbell squeezed between the feet, bend the knees to curl it back under the bench. A machine "seated leg curl" exists (ankle pad, no dumbbell) and a "seated dumbbell curl" exists (biceps, dumbbells in the hands) -- this card may be conflating one of those names with the prone dumbbell-between-feet mechanic rather than describing a real, independently-documented exercise. Not a confident fix: I have no sourced correct version of a SEATED dumbbell-between-feet leg curl to propose in its place, and cannot rule out that it is a genuine, just rarely-documented, home variant. Flagging rather than guessing.

Confirms FINDINGS.md F22: both sources describe the back foot straight behind the front foot, toes near the front heel, ~80-90% load on the front leg -- the same mechanic as the shipped dumbbell-b-stance-rdl card. The card's own cue/description is accurate (verdict ok), but this and dumbbell-b-stance-rdl appear to be the same real exercise shipped twice under two names. See FINDINGS.md F23.

audited.problem: Both sources describe the GHR as driven by active knee extension on the way down and knee flexion on the way up -- the knee bend is what distinguishes a true glute-ham raise from a plain back extension / reverse hyper. The shipped description omits the knee action entirely, describing only a torso lower-and-raise, which reads as a pure hip hinge.

proposed.cue: Anchor your feet, extend your knees to lower down, then bend your knees to pull yourself back up.
proposed.description: Set up in the glute-ham bench with your ankles anchored and thighs on the pad. Lower your torso forward by extending your knees until your body is nearly straight, then pull yourself back up by bending your knees and squeezing your hamstrings, finishing with a glute squeeze. It's the knee bend that drives you up, not a hip hinge alone -- this one is advanced, so ease in.
